_meta.name: English
site.rakhigarhi.name: Rakhigarhi
site.rakhigarhi.period: A Harappan city, about 4,500 years ago
site.rakhigarhi.quote: Always dig down, never sideways. The layers are our clock. Dig from the side and you break it.
site.rakhigarhi.para1: This is Rakhigarhi in Haryana. Four thousand years ago it was one of the biggest cities in the world. Most of it still lies under a wheat field.
site.rakhigarhi.para2: Your trench is small. Six things are buried near here. Find them all. The last one is cut into the bottom of the mound.
site.rakhigarhi.keynote: The grave has not been touched. She lies exactly where they put her. Dr Kaul stops talking, which never happens.
site.rakhigarhi.close: We fill the trench in again. Everything you found goes to the store with its layer number. Without that number, an object is just a pretty thing.
site.lothal.name: Lothal
site.lothal.period: A Harappan port, about 4,400 years ago
site.lothal.quote: Everyone comes to Lothal to argue about the big brick tank. Dig the workshop first. The workshop paid for the tank.
site.lothal.para1: Lothal is small and flat and very hot. Long ago the sea came much closer. This little town made things and sold them overseas.
site.lothal.para2: Your trench cuts the workshop and touches the edge of the great tank. Work slowly. The bead waste here is smaller than a grain of rice.
site.lothal.keynote: You have found the gate where water went in. Was it a dock for ships, or a tank to hold water? The bricks will not say, and nor will anyone honest.
site.lothal.close: Lothal closes with the whole bead story in the record. Raw stone, drill, waste, finished bead. That story is worth more than any single object.
site.vidisha.name: Vidisha
site.vidisha.period: A Mauryan town, about 2,300 years ago
site.vidisha.quote: You are digging a crossroads, not a city. Two rivers, one road to Ujjain, and everybody's stone ends up here.
site.vidisha.para1: Vidisha sits where two rivers meet, on the main road south. The great gateways at Sanchi, nine kilometres away, were carved by workers from this town.
site.vidisha.para2: Your trench cuts a merchant street. Under the later floors are the Mauryan levels. Under those is a black shiny pottery that dates a layer on sight.
site.vidisha.keynote: The base of the pillar is still standing where it was set. A Greek ambassador put it up, and wrote his name on it in an Indian language.
site.vidisha.close: Vidisha goes back under sheeting and soil. We record the pillar base exactly where it lay. Move it first and you lose half of what it tells you.
site.nalanda.name: Nalanda
site.nalanda.quote: Nine buildings, one plan, seven hundred years of rebuilding on the same spot. Every floor you cut through is somebody's whole life.
site.nalanda.para1: Nalanda was a university. Students came from Tibet, China, Korea and South East Asia. A Chinese monk called Xuanzang studied here and wrote down what he saw.
site.nalanda.para2: Your trench takes a block of monks' rooms down to the oldest floor. Below that there is ash. The ash is why this place is famous.
site.nalanda.keynote: Palm leaf, burnt black, still holding its shape. Then the trowel touches it and it is only a dark shadow in the soil. Now the shadow is the document.
site.nalanda.close: We lift the leaf inside a block of soil and send it to the lab. Some finds are dug in a trench. Some are dug later, under a microscope.
site.hampi.name: Hampi
site.hampi.period: The city of Vijayanagara, 500 years ago
site.hampi.quote: Here the disaster is near the top and the city is underneath it. Read it downwards and you read a life backwards.
site.hampi.para1: Vijayanagara was one of the largest cities in the world in the 1500s. It spread over 26 square kilometres of rock and river.
site.hampi.para2: This is your last trench of the year. It cuts a rich house, through the ash of 1565, and down into the floors below it.
site.hampi.keynote: The pot was put under the floor on purpose. Somebody hid it and meant to come back for it. They never did.
site.hampi.close: We count, weigh and photograph the hoard in the trench before one coin is lifted. A hoard is something that happened, not just a pile of gold.
find.rakhigarhi.1.no: People here wore clay bangles. Rich and poor, everybody. They were baked in ovens by the thousand. Ordinary things like this tell us more about daily life than gold does.
find.rakhigarhi.2.no: Somebody fished here. The copper came from hills far away to the south. The metalworkers had their own part of the town.
find.rakhigarhi.3.no: A cube of hard stone for weighing goods. Traders 350 kilometres away used exactly the same weights. Somebody was making sure everyone weighed the same way.
find.rakhigarhi.4.no: A covered drain that ran under the street. Every brick is the same shape. These people built drains before they built palaces.
find.rakhigarhi.5.no: A small stone stamp. It shows an animal with one horn and a row of signs. Nobody can read Indus writing. We know about 400 signs and we have no way in.
find.rakhigarhi.6.no: A woman buried with pots by her head. In 2019 scientists tested DNA from a woman in this cemetery. Her family came from local farmers and from Iran. That is one person, and people still argue about what it means.
find.lothal.1.no: Beads of carnelian, a hard red stone. They were heated, drilled, and painted with white lines. Beads like these have been found in Iraq, 2,000 kilometres away.
find.lothal.2.no: The drill had to be harder than the bead. Drilling one long bead took more than a day of turning. Only Harappan workshops used this stone.
find.lothal.3.nm: Clay game pieces and a dice
find.lothal.3.no: Playing pieces and a dice with one to six dots, in the same pattern we use now. Games are one of the few things we can say for certain these people did.
find.lothal.4.no: Grains of rice pressed into wet mud, then dried. People here ate rice, wheat and barley.
find.lothal.5.no: A round stamp of a kind used in Bahrain, found on an Indian shore. Clay tablets in Iraq talk about trading with a land called Meluhha. Most people think that means the Indus.
find.lothal.6.nm: The gate of the great tank
find.lothal.6.no: A brick tank 214 metres long, with a channel in and a gate out. Some say it was a dock for ships. Others say it held water. The bricks are certain. What they were for is not.
find.vidisha.1.no: A fine black tableware used in the big northern cities. It shines like glass. One piece tells you the age of a layer straight away.
find.vidisha.2.no: Silver stamped with a sun, a hill and other marks, punched in one at a time. This is India's first money. It has no king's face and no writing on it.
find.vidisha.3.no: The ivory carvers of Vidisha worked as a guild. They carved a great gateway at Sanchi and wrote their names on it. That is a workman signing his work.
find.vidisha.4.no: A waste chip with a mirror shine on one face. The stone was cut hundreds of kilometres away and carried here. Nobody is sure how they got that shine.
find.vidisha.5.no: The emperor Ashoka had his orders cut into rock so they would last. They did. But nobody could read the letters for 1,500 years, until James Prinsep worked them out in 1837.
find.vidisha.6.no: Heliodorus came from a Greek kingdom as an ambassador. He set up this pillar for an Indian god and called himself a follower. A Greek, writing in an Indian language, to an Indian god.
find.nalanda.1.no: Lime plaster shaped over a brick core, and once painted. Whole walls of these figures ran along the outside of the buildings.
find.nalanda.2.no: A clay seal with the name of the monastery on it. Seals like this told the diggers which mound they were standing on.
find.nalanda.3.no: Cast in bronze using wax. Bronzes from this school reached Tibet and Java. Monks carried them, not traders.
find.nalanda.4.no: Soot is still on the lip. Xuanzang wrote that lamps burned all night in the halls where the monks argued. This one sat in a hole in a wall.
find.nalanda.5.nm: Copper sheet with a royal grant
find.nalanda.5.no: A king of Sumatra paid for a building here. An Indian king wrote the gift down on copper. Bihar and Indonesia, on one sheet of metal.
find.nalanda.6.no: The library burned. A Persian book written 200 years later describes an army destroying a monastery, but historians argue over which one. The ash layer is the better witness, and it is thick.
find.hampi.1.no: Charcoal spread over a burnt floor. After the battle of Talikota in 1565, the city was destroyed over several months. The burnt layer is thick enough to dig slowly.
find.hampi.2.no: Green glazed pottery from China, carried by sea and then 350 kilometres inland. A broken foreign pot is the cheapest proof of a trade route.
find.hampi.3.no: Waste from a blacksmith on the market street. You can still trace the market streets running out from the temple gates.
find.hampi.4.no: Cut from granite and then left. The famous stone chariot at Hampi has wheels like this one, carved separately and fitted on.
find.hampi.5.no: The empire bought war horses by the thousand through the coast. A Portuguese visitor in about 1520 thought the city was as big as Rome.
find.hampi.6.no: Gold coins stamped with a boar, buried under a house floor and never dug up again. People hide gold when they expect to come back for it.
quest.rakhigarhi.question: A woman is buried at the edge of this mound, with pots by her head. Her city used things made hundreds of kilometres away. How far did they travel? And who made sure nobody cheated?
quest.rakhigarhi.answer: Weights that match a city 350 kilometres away. Bricks the same shape as bricks in Pakistan. Writing that nobody can read. The same rules held right across a thousand kilometres. Somebody was making that happen.
quest.rakhigarhi.clue.1.text: Bangles are baked in a hot oven. The oven burns the ground red, and it stays red for ever. Look for red ground. Take the grass off it.
quest.rakhigarhi.clue.1.why: Baked clay needs an oven. Ovens burn the earth.
quest.rakhigarhi.clue.2.text: A fish hook is no use without water. There was a pond here once, and the ground still dips. Cut into the edge of the low ground.
quest.rakhigarhi.clue.2.why: Things stay where people used them.
quest.rakhigarhi.clue.3.text: Traders weigh what they sell. The stack of stones marks the old road. The market stood under it. Go deeper than the pond.
quest.rakhigarhi.clue.3.why: A road brings a market. A market needs weights.
quest.rakhigarhi.clue.4.text: A buried wall pushes its bricks up to the surface. Follow the line of bricks and dig straight down. The drain runs under the street.
quest.rakhigarhi.clue.5.text: Seals are kept where goods are stored. The lone tamarind grows on the highest floor of the old town. Dig under the tree.
quest.rakhigarhi.clue.5.why: The deeper the floor, the older the town.
quest.rakhigarhi.clue.6.text: Graves go outside the walls, never inside. Thorn trees took the ground nobody would build on. Go deeper than you have all season.
quest.rakhigarhi.clue.6.why: The dead are buried away from the living.
quest.lothal.question: A brick tank longer than two football pitches sits beside a town of bead makers. Was it a dock for ships, or a tank for water? And what did this town sell to afford either one?
quest.lothal.answer: Red stone beads, drilled with a stone harder than anything nearby, and shipped 2,000 kilometres west. Seals came back the other way. Whether the tank held ships or water is still argued. What it stood next to is not.
quest.lothal.clue.1.text: A bead workshop throws away far more stone than it sells. Look for pale chips on the flat ground. Lift the sand off them.
quest.lothal.clue.1.why: Making things leaves waste. Waste is evidence.
quest.lothal.clue.2.text: The drill that makes a bead is harder than the bead. It snaps, and it goes out with the broken pots. Dig the broken pots.
quest.lothal.clue.2.why: Rubbish heaps are where tools go to be found.
quest.lothal.clue.3.text: People play where they live. The low mud-brick platform is a house floor. Take it down into the room below.
quest.lothal.clue.3.why: A floor seals whatever was dropped on it.
quest.lothal.clue.4.text: Rice needs standing water, and this ground was drained by hand. The dry ditch is where the water ran. Cut its bank.
quest.lothal.clue.4.why: Crops follow water. Water follows engineering.
quest.lothal.clue.5.text: Goods off a ship go into a store, and a store is locked with a seal. The line of bricks is a warehouse wall. Go under its floor.
quest.lothal.clue.5.why: Seals belong where goods are kept.
quest.lothal.clue.6.text: The white salt patch is where the water stood longest. The tank wall is under you, and its gate is under that. This is the deepest thing here.
quest.lothal.clue.6.why: The biggest building has the deepest base.
quest.vidisha.question: Long ago a Greek ambassador set up a pillar here. It was for an Indian god, and he called himself a follower. What sort of town made that seem completely normal?
quest.vidisha.answer: A crossroads. Fine city pottery. The first coins. A guild of ivory carvers who signed a monument. Stone hauled in from hundreds of kilometres away. And a foreign ambassador who found the local god perfectly ordinary. Busy roads make strangers normal.
quest.vidisha.clue.1.text: Fine plates break like any others. The broken pots are where the town threw its rubbish. The shiny black ware is just under the grass.
quest.vidisha.clue.1.why: One kind of pot can date a whole layer.
quest.vidisha.clue.2.text: Coins get dropped where people stop and pay. The stack of stones stands where two tracks cross. Dig where they meet.
quest.vidisha.clue.2.why: Money is lost at markets and gates.
quest.vidisha.clue.3.text: Carvers work in a workshop, and a workshop has a floor. The low mud-brick platform is one. The tools are in it.
quest.vidisha.clue.3.why: Craft workers cluster together and stay put.
quest.vidisha.clue.4.text: Shaping stone makes chips. Imperial stone makes chips with a mirror shine. Take the spread of chips down to the Mauryan level.
quest.vidisha.clue.4.why: That shine belongs to one century only.
quest.vidisha.clue.5.text: An order is cut into rock so it will last, and rock is where you find it. The big rocks carry it. Dig beside them.
quest.vidisha.clue.5.why: Notices are put where people walk past.
quest.vidisha.clue.6.text: The broken post on the rise is not natural. Under it is the base it stood in, and the writing runs round the base. Go deep.
quest.vidisha.clue.6.why: A pillar's story is in its foot.
quest.nalanda.question: Seven hundred years of monastery, and then a layer of ash. What was kept here that made burning it worth the trouble?
quest.nalanda.answer: A library, and a network. Seals with the monastery's name on them. A gift paid for by a king in Sumatra. Bronzes that reached Tibet. And one burnt palm leaf, which is the only part of the library anybody will ever hold.
quest.nalanda.clue.1.text: The outer wall carried rows of clay figures. The line of bricks is that wall. The figures fell just inside it.
quest.nalanda.clue.1.why: Decoration falls where the wall stood.
quest.nalanda.clue.2.text: Every letter leaving a monastery is sealed with its name. The broken pots are where broken seals ended up. It is shallow.
quest.nalanda.clue.2.why: A seal tells you which mound you are standing on.
quest.nalanda.clue.3.text: A shrine holds the statues. The low platform is its floor. The bronze is under it.
quest.nalanda.clue.4.text: Monks read at night and lamps go out. The dip in the ground was the water tank, and the rooms stood along its edge. Cut into the bank.
quest.nalanda.clue.4.why: People dig water where they live beside it.
quest.nalanda.clue.5.text: A royal gift is written on copper and kept where the community met. The row of stone posts is the courtyard. Go under it.
quest.nalanda.clue.5.why: Important papers are stored at the centre.
quest.nalanda.clue.6.text: The black burnt floor is why this place is famous. Everything under it burned. Go through the ash and keep going. This is the deepest cut of the season.
quest.nalanda.clue.6.why: A burnt layer seals everything below it.
quest.hampi.question: The biggest city in India in 1565, and empty a year later. Somebody buried a pot of gold under a floor here. What happened to them?
quest.hampi.answer: A battle, then months of destruction. The ash sits near the top and the city lies underneath it, so you read this place backwards. The gold was never dug up again. People bury gold when they expect to come back.
quest.hampi.clue.1.text: Start with the disaster, because here it is the shallowest thing on the site. The black burnt floor is the burning. Barely scratch it.
quest.hampi.clue.1.why: At Hampi the disaster lies above the city.
quest.hampi.clue.2.text: Foreign pottery travelled 350 kilometres inland to be dropped in a market. Dig the broken pots.
quest.hampi.clue.2.why: Foreign pots prove a trade route.
quest.hampi.clue.3.text: A market has a blacksmith, and a blacksmith makes waste that never rots. The black heap is exactly what it looks like.
quest.hampi.clue.3.why: Waste marks where work was done.
quest.hampi.clue.4.text: The chariot wheels were cut from granite on the spot. The big rocks are the quarry. A rejected wheel lies beside them.
quest.hampi.clue.4.why: Quarries keep the pieces that failed.
quest.hampi.clue.5.text: The empire bought war horses by the thousand. The row of stone posts is the market where they were traded. Go under the street.
quest.hampi.clue.5.why: The market is where the money moved.
quest.hampi.clue.6.text: Somebody lifted a floor slab in a good house and hid a pot of gold. They meant to come back. The house platform is still there. This is the deepest cut of the year.
quest.hampi.clue.6.why: You hide gold under a floor you trust.
ui.title: Dig for Bharat
ui.tagline: Five digs. Thirty real things. Every one tells you when it comes from.
ui.confirm_new: Start again from the beginning? You will lose what you have done.
ui.confirm_leave: Leave the dig and go back to the start?
ui.all_done: All six found. Press R to finish.
ui.loading_note: Making the land, then putting five layers of earth under every step of it.
ui.expect_depth: Look about {n} m down, in layer {layer}.
tool.trowel.help: Slow and safe. Use it near anything fragile.
tool.shovel.help: Fast in soft earth only. Lifts two loads at a time.
tool.pick.help: Three times as fast in hard earth. It can break what you find.
tool.brush.help: Picks up a find without hurting it.
tool.dental.help: Slower, but a careful lift is worth more points.
tool.survey.help: Four uses. Points the way to what the clue wants.
station.sieve.help: Eight loads of earth. Finds small things you missed.
station.float.help: Twelve loads. Finds seeds and charcoal.
station.station.help: Shows you where the clue points.
toast.season_open: Dig {name} is open. Six clues in your notebook. Press J to read them.
toast.close: The soil changes here. Darker, and it breaks differently. You are close.
toast.something: Something is coming up in layer {layer}. Change to the brush, or the fine pick if it looks delicate.
toast.broke: {name} broke under the pick. The repair bench can mend most of it.
toast.no_spoil: No dug earth to put back. Dig something first.
toast.wrong_tool: A spade will not cut {name}. Use the trowel or the pick.
toast.deep: Too deep to climb out. Face the wall and hold jump. Or press F to fly up and look.
toast.float: Out of the water tank: {thing}. This is what people ate.
toast.bench: {name} is mended. Most of its value is back. The break stays in the record, because it happened.
toast.bench_none: Nothing needs mending. That is what the brush is for.
toast.station: The clue points {dir}, about {dist} steps away, {depth} m down.
toast.hint: That earth is not from here. What the clue wants is {dir}, about {dist} steps, {depth} m down.
toast.finder_here: The signal is right under you. Dig down about {depth} m.
toast.finder_none: No uses left. The survey stand can still point for you.
toast.station_far: Take the dug earth to a station near the marker post.
toast.fly_on: Flying. Space goes up, C goes down.
report.title: Dig finished
report.fail1: Your energy is gone and the question is still open. Everything you found is recorded. The rest stays in the ground until next year.
report.fail2: Next time: read the clue before you dig. Use the finder if you are not sure. Keep the pick away from anything delicate.
sieve.8: only grit, which is also an answer
float.1: wheat and barley, and one grain of rice
float.3: charcoal, enough to get a date
float.4: weed seeds from a farmed field
float.6: insect remains, so there was standing water
howto.1.p: The clue tells you what to look for.
howto.2.p: Walk about and look for the thing in the clue.
howto.3.p: Hold the left button. The block cracks, then breaks.
howto.4.p: Deeper earth is older. A thing only shows up in its own layer.
howto.5.p: When something appears, swap to the brush. The pick will break it.
howto.6.p: Right click to fill a hole, or to build a step.
howto.7.p: Face the wall and hold jump. Press F to fly up and look.
howto.8.p: Sieve your dug earth. It finds small things.
about.1.p: Every object and every note is a real find. Where experts still argue, the game says so.
about.2.p: Every picture is drawn by the game when it starts. Every sound is made by the game as you play.
about.3.p: Each dig has its own raga. The drums only play while you are digging.
about.4.p: three.js and Electron, both free and open. No part of Minecraft is used here.
toast.then: This is the city as it stood. Walk about and look. Press T to come back.
toast.now: Back to the dig. The city is under your feet now.
toast.no_dig_then: You cannot dig in the past. Press T to go back to the dig.
howto.9.p: Press T. The city appears as it stood. Press T again to dig.
